questions.explain: gp2 allocates 3 IOPS per GB (min 100, max 16,000 — the ceiling hits at ~5,334 GB). Volumes under 1 TB accumulate burst credits for 3,000 IOPS; when credits exhaust (roughly 30 minutes at full burst for a 100 GB volume), performance collapses to the 300 IOPS baseline silently.
options: 3 IOPS per GB (minimum 100, maximum 16,000); volumes under 1 TB burst to 3,000 IOPS on credits, then drop to the baseline silently when credits exhaust
Fixed 3,000 IOPS on every volume regardless of size, with no burst mechanism
IOPS tied to instance class rather than volume size
5 IOPS per GB with burst up to 10,000 IOPS for volumes under 500 GB
questions.q: How does gp2 allocate IOPS and what is the burst credit trap?

questions.explain: gp3 decouples IOPS from storage size: every volume gets 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s throughput in the base price, provisionable to 16,000 IOPS / 1,000 MB/s — no burst credits, no storage floor for an IOPS target.
options: It includes automatic tiering between gp3 and io2
It provides sub-millisecond P99 latency guarantees
It offers higher maximum IOPS than io1 at a lower price
It decouples IOPS from storage size — 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s included in the base price regardless of volume size, with no burst credits or silent collapse
questions.q: What is the single architectural difference that makes gp3 the better default over gp2?

questions.explain: io1 allows up to 64,000 IOPS but with a 50 IOPS-per-GB ratio constraint: 64,000 IOPS requires at least 1,280 GB of storage even if the data is smaller — the 'storage tax'.
options: io1 has a lower IOPS ceiling than gp3 but better durability
io1's maximum IOPS-to-storage ratio of 50:1 forces over-provisioning storage to reach high IOPS — the 'storage tax'
io1 includes free throughput while gp3 charges for it
io1 durability is 99.999%, identical to io2
questions.q: What is the io1 'storage tax' and what causes it?

questions.explain: io2 keeps io1's per-IOPS pricing but raises durability to 99.999% (100x io1) and the ratio to 500:1 — 64,000 IOPS needs only 128 GB, eliminating most of the storage tax.
options: io2 is being deprecated in favor of io1 for new provisioning
io2 has the same durability as io1 but a lower IOPS ceiling
io2 improves durability to 99.999% and the IOPS-to-storage ratio to 500:1 at the same per-IOPS price as io1
io2 charges per million I/O requests instead of per provisioned IOPS
questions.q: Why is io2 strictly better than io1 for new provisioning?

questions.explain: Provisioned IOPS is warranted above gp3's 16,000 IOPS ceiling, for latency-sensitive consistent I/O, or compliance-mandated guarantees; it's overkill for any workload under 16,000 sustained IOPS (including read-heavy workloads absorbed by caches).
options: Workloads needing more than 16,000 IOPS (gp3's ceiling), consistent low-latency guarantees, or documented performance for compliance — overkill under 16,000 sustained IOPS
All production OLTP workloads regardless of IOPS
Any volume larger than 1 TB
Any workload exceeding 3,000 sustained IOPS
questions.q: When does provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) actually make sense, and when is it overkill?
